title: Git & GitHub: Version Control for Your Code

intro.text: AI coding assistants can write — and rewrite — a lot of code very quickly. As the person directing that work, you can only delegate that power safely if you can rewind any change that goes wrong. This chapter introduces version control with Git, gets it installed on your machine, and walks you through saving snapshots of your project, publishing it to GitHub, and syncing work between computers. For a manager, the commit history is also your audit trail — it shows exactly what the AI changed and when. Along the way you'll see why version control is the safety net that lets you confidently hand more permissions to an AI assistant like Claude Code.

intro.title: Before you continue
intro.text: Lessons 5.2 and 5.3 cover Git installation on different operating systems — work through the one that matches your laptop.

lessons.title: Version Control
lessons.objective: Understand version control well enough to insist on it before any AI coding begins — and to spot when a project is missing this safety net. Along the way, get to know Git, the tool that dominates the field.

blocks.text: Think back to the last time you worked on a big class presentation. Your backup folder probably ended up looking something like this:
EventPlan.pptx
EventPlan_edited.pptx
EventPlan_final.pptx
EventPlan_final_v2.pptx  ← the “real” final… for now

Copying a file and stretching the name — final.pptx, final_edited.pptx, REAL_final.pptx — is a homemade version-control system. Version control applies that same instinct to code files, but does it properly:
As development moves forward, code is constantly added, changed, and deleted.
Saving the state of your project at any moment you choose — like a checkpoint in a video game — is what version control does.

Git organizes that flow into a clean commit history: every version of the same project stacks up one line at a time, and you can jump back to any point whenever you want. Instead of four confusingly named copies, you get one tidy list like this:

rows: fix: correct typos in the schedule
init: first draft of the event plan

blocks.text: “Git manages your changes as a clean commit history — every version in one stack, and you can roll back to any point at any time.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

steps.title: Why you need version control (especially with AI)

blocks.text: Version control has always mattered, but three reasons make it especially important when the actual coding is done by an AI assistant you direct.
1. You can roll back the AI's mistakes
When bugs pile up or the AI writes something completely off the rails, you can quickly return to the last point where everything worked.
2. You can painlessly discard changes you don't like
No need to hunt through multiple files deleting code line by line — just move back to the version before that feature went in.
3. You can safely delegate more authority to the AI
Even if you hand file-editing permissions over to the AI, there's a safety net: if something goes wrong, you can always restore a previous version.
Git is a version control program created by Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux. More than 90% of developers worldwide use it.
It adds version control to any folder you choose: save a version at any point, or roll back to an earlier one.
Starting with the next lesson, we'll install Git and use it hands-on. Follow the installation lesson for your operating system.

blocks.text: Click Source Control in the left sidebar. Hover over Changes and click + to stage the files you want to include.
Staging selects the changes to include in your next commit, like putting items in a shopping cart before checkout.
“Stage → write a message → commit. This flow is the backbone of every version you'll ever record.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: Describe in one line what this change is. For a first version, something as simple as INIT is fine. Good messages become signposts later, when you're walking back up the graph looking for a specific point in time.
Click Commit (the check mark).
Your new commit appears in the Source Control graph.

steps.title: How big should a commit be?

blocks.text: Commit often, in small, single-feature units — not giant batches. For example, if the AI is building authentication, have it commit login → sign-up → password reset separately. Then, if one feature breaks, you can roll back just that point without losing the rest. This is also the standard to hold your AI assistant to: one feature per commit keeps every change small enough for you to review.

blocks.title: Only when you need to undo a mistake
blocks.text: Read this as a recovery guide. Do not discard or revert working project files just to complete this page.
Discard — cancel changes that aren't committed yet

Discard removes uncommitted changes from the selected files. Review the files first: this can permanently remove work that Git has never saved. For tracked files, discard restores their latest committed version. Do not discard unrelated work.
Revert — undo a mistake that was already committed
If the bad code was already committed, git revert creates a new commit that cancels it out. Two steps:
Copy the bad commit's ID from the graph — right-click the commit in the Source Control graph (or use the ... button next to it) to open the menu, then choose Copy Commit ID.

blocks.title: Revert that commit only if needed

blocks.text: Run git revert with the actual commit ID, replacing the placeholder below. Git normally creates a new commit that reverses the selected commit. If a conflict occurs, resolve it before completing the revert.
git revert <copied-commit-ID>
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.text: If a commit-message editor opens, save the message and close that editor so Git can finish. Check the Source Control graph for the new revert commit. If Git reports a conflict, do not assume the revert is finished.
git reset can move the current branch and, depending on its options, discard working files. This course uses revert for changes that have already been committed.

lessons.title: Meet GitHub & Publish Your Project
lessons.objective: Understand GitHub, the Git-based online code storage service, publish your own project to it for the first time — and confirm the full history made the trip.

blocks.text: GitHub hosts Git repositories online so you can back up and share code and its history.
It stores your computer's code files online — together with the entire version history that Git manages.
In other words, it's not simple file upload; it's a service for sharing your Git repository as-is.

steps.title: Not just source code — your Git versions come along

blocks.text: GitHub doesn't hold just your source code; it also stores the full version history you've been managing with Git. That's where the name comes from: the hub for Git (Git + Hub) — GitHub.
“A repository that lives on a remote server like GitHub is called a remote repository.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: Backup
Even if your local folder is deleted, you can pull the code and the version history back down from GitHub.
Multiple computers & collaboration
Moving between a school lab machine and your laptop, or working with teammates, it's easy for everyone to share the same project.
Connecting outside services
Some services can deploy directly from a GitHub repository. Connecting Supabase to your app is a separate step; a GitHub sign-in alone does not connect the database.
Use the GitHub account you prepared in Lesson 5.2 or 5.3. Already signed in at https://github.com/login? Continue to the next step. VS Code may still request authorization when you publish.
You are signed in to the GitHub account you prepared earlier.

steps.title: Publish your local repository to GitHub

blocks.text: In the Source Control tab (Graph view), click the blue Publish Branch button.
The first time, GitHub login and a VS Code authorization step (Authorize) run in order. If email verification is requested, complete that too.

blocks.title: Name the repository and choose its visibility

blocks.text: In the input box at the top, type a repository name (e.g. pomodoro-timer-web). Avoid spaces and special characters (except - and _), and stick to English letters and digits.
Choose the visibility required for your course project. Public repositories are visible to everyone. Private repositories are visible only to people with access.
Finally, one more login may pop up to connect the Git program with GitHub (“Sign in with your browser”) — go ahead and finish it.
Publishing finishes without an error. Check the repository on GitHub in the next Check the result step.
Version history usually runs in a single line, but when you need experiments or forks in the road, you can split it into branches.
The main branch is a common starting branch name. Publish Branch uploads the branch you are currently using; that branch is not always named main.

blocks.title: Find your project and its commits

blocks.text: On GitHub, open your profile menu (top right) → Your repositories to find the repository you just uploaded. On the repository page, click the Commits link near the top — you'll see every version you've committed so far, carried over intact.
GitHub shows your project files and commit history.

lessons.title: Using GitHub: Push, Pull, and Clone
lessons.objective: Get hands-on with the three core commands for working with a repository on GitHub — Push, Pull, and Clone — and learn to read at a glance whether local and remote are in sync.

blocks.text: Local repository: the project folder that exists only on your computer.
Remote repository: the copy uploaded online, e.g. on GitHub (usually referred to as origin).

In VS Code's Graph view, main marks your latest local commit, while origin/main marks the latest remote commit. When those two labels sit on different commits, the two sides need to be synchronized. That pair of labels is a manager's fastest status check: if they've drifted apart, some work isn't backed up — or isn't shared — yet.
Pushing sends commits you created locally up to the remote.
In VS Code Source Control, use Push to upload your local commits. Sync Changes combines a pull and a push, so it can also bring remote changes into your project.
If a pull/push confirmation dialog appears, click OK.
“Make it a habit to push right after every new commit. Your local and remote history stay identical at all times.”
blocks.title: Another way to think about it

blocks.text: Push finishes successfully and GitHub shows your latest commit.
Pulling brings down commits that were added from another computer (or from GitHub's web editor) into your local copy.
Example scenario: you edit a file directly on github.com and commit it with “Commit changes”; back on your machine, you Pull to fetch that commit.

blocks.title: Pull when the remote has newer commits

blocks.text: Click the arrow icon on the right side of the Source Control graph → Pull.
The remote changes are now present locally, or Git reports that you are already up to date.

steps.title: Clone — copy an entire remote to a new local machine

blocks.title: Only on a computer without this project
blocks.text: Keep working in your existing project for this course. Clone only when you need another local copy.
Use clone when the project folder doesn't exist at all — for example, when you start working on a new computer.
On the GitHub repository page, click the green Code button → copy the clone URL.
The command below is a pattern. Before running it, replace both placeholders and move to your webdev folder as explained below.
git clone <copied-URL> <local-folder-name>
blocks.label: Terminal command
blocks.note: Paste into the named input area. Press Enter to run.

blocks.title: Move to webdev, then run your completed clone command

blocks.text: Replace PASTE_FULL_PATH_TO_WEBDEV_HERE with your actual folder path, keeping the quotation marks.
Example locations from the guidebook: ~/webdev on Mac and C:\webdev on Windows. Use the actual location of your own workspace.
cd "PASTE_FULL_PATH_TO_WEBDEV_HERE"
blocks.label: Terminal command

blocks.title: Example only — use your own repository URL

blocks.text: Example — download the project into a folder named pomodoro under your web-dev folder:
git clone https://github.com/user/pomodoro-timer-web.git pomodoro
blocks.label: Example only
blocks.note: Replace the example URL with your own repository URL before using it.

blocks.text: When the command finishes, every file and the full version history of the remote repository comes back down to your local machine.

rows: A new commit appeared on the remote
You need the whole project from scratch

lessons.title: Safely Granting Permissions to AI
lessons.objective: With Git in place as a safety device, learn how to safely grant Claude Code broader permissions — and how to verify the guardrails actually trigger.

steps.title: Why hand over permissions at all?

blocks.text: Claude Code uses permission settings to decide which actions need approval. Git gives you saved checkpoints, but it does not protect work that has never been committed. Review the changes before allowing broader editing permissions.

blocks.title: Reference: bypass mode — not used in this course

blocks.text: 1. bypass permissions mode (not recommended)
The simplest — and riskiest — approach is to skip every permission check:
claude --permission-mode bypassPermissions
blocks.label: Reference example

blocks.text: Bypass mode skips many permission checks. We do not use it for the course exercises.
We won't use this mode while you're learning.
In your project folder, create a folder named .claude if it does not exist. Inside it, create settings.json. If you already have this file, review its existing settings before making changes.

blocks.label: File contents

blocks.text: The settings are saved in .claude/settings.json inside this project.

defaultMode: "acceptEdits" allows file edits and some common file operations in the permitted workspace without asking each time. Other behavior depends on the command, permission rules, and current Claude Code version.
The ask array — registers commands that must get your approval before running.
Bash(...) matches commands run through Claude Code’s Bash tool. PowerShell tool commands need their own matching rules.
* is a wildcard that matches whatever arguments follow.

These sample rules cover the listed Bash command patterns. They are not a universal block on every possible command or tool. Check the current permissions documentation and review any requested action.
